newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thai bargains emerge but stock index still weak.
newsitem.headline: Thai bargains emerge but stock index still weak.

text.p: Foreign funds, which are expected to decide the end of Thailand's long, painful stock market slide, said on Tuesday that while a few bargains had emerged, the broad market sell-off would continue.
"The bottom of the market is going to be reached within the next six months but we don't think it's been reached yet," said Stewart Aldcroft, sales director at Templeton in Hong Kong.
"But there are some stocks that are now significantly underpriced, and that has led us to start buying one or two."
The SETI has shed half its value in the past 12 months, leading some players to ask how much further it can fall.
"It's certainly closer to bottoming, but we're not there yet," said one Asian fund manager who declined to be identified.
"We have a very low exposure to Thailand and we don't think it's time to increase that exposure yet."

The Stock Exchange of Thailand Index (SETI) plunged more than three percent in trading on Tuesday on expectations of a radical shake-up in the country's financial services sector, which accounts for more than 35 percent of the index.

In a long-anticipated move to bolster the shaky industry, Thailand's central bank on Monday ordered banks and finance firms to raise provisions for sub-standard loans and asked 10 troubled finance companies to raise capital immediately.
It was the government's first admission of a critical problem confronting Thailand's economy and prompted speculation of an immediate wave of consolidation in the sector.

The SETI recovered some ground by the end of Tuesday to close down 18.50 points points or 2.62 percent at 688.74. Late buying of bank and finance stocks, which fell sharply at the open after being suspended while Monday's announcement was made, aided in the recovery.

The threat of a sovereign debt rating downgrade by ratings agency Moody's Investors Service Inc still hung over the market, and while the economy was showing signs of improvement there had been little concrete growth to lift the stock market.

"Our view is still negative," said Annabel Betz, senior economist at ING Barings. "There are obviously persistent concerns about asset quality that will delay recovery in sentiment and the trend in interest rates will compound the problems of economic recovery."
Thailand's government has said recently that interest rates would be kept high to counter speculative selling of the baht.

However, Thailand's massive current account deficit has shown signs of improvement. The latest current account data showed the deficit at 19.1 billion baht in December, down from a peak of 49.6 billion baht in April 1996.
"And if there starts to be a perception that the government is addressing some of these problems, then of course it will relieve some of the pressure," Betz said.

In the meantime, funds said they were looking for undervalued export- or consumer-oriented stocks which had been dragged down with the market despite an absence of exposure to the country's troubled financial services or property sectors.
"It is a stock-pickers market right now," said Aldcroft.
Traders said it was too early to assess the impact of recent developments, but as the situation became more clear the appearance of the Bangkok market would change significantly.

"This market is going to get looked at very, very carefully by the institutions who are going to go away and do their homework and decide what is good value, what is bad value, and then have a look at quality of assets," one head trader said.
"I think we're going to get a very two-tiered market."
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6470
